and sent and took captive the Arabs who were in Cyprus.
And because of this, Muhammad, the emir of the island of Qardu (Jazirat Ibn Umar), entered Cappadocia,
and the Romans and the Slavs met him,
and the Romans were defeated near Caesarea.
And the Slavs made peace with the Arabs,
and went out with them to Syria, about seven thousand of them.
And they settled them in Antioch and Cyrrhus,
and gave them wives and provisions.
Now Justinian, just as he did not keep the oaths with the Arabs,
also began to kill the magnates of the Romans.
And for this reason, they gathered against him and seized him,
and slit his nose,
and made a man named Leontius king in the year 1007
1007 of the Greeks (696 AD?).
And in that same year, the emir of the city of Jazira impaled the leaders unjustly:
Simeon bar Nawla, a weaver,
and Mardanshah and his son, who were from Nisibis.
And after a year, the Arabs began to mint dinars, zuzas, and fulus with inscriptions only, without images.
And in the year 1010,
1010, there came the general of Cilicia whose name was Apsimar, who was called Tiberius,
and he overthrew Leontius from the kingdom,
and reigned in his place,
yet he did not kill him.
This same Tiberius again subdued the Slavs who had rebelled against the Romans.
And he went out to the territory of Samosata, and they killed (or: he killed?) five thousand Arabs,
and took captives and plundered, and returned.
Now Abd al-Malik appointed two army commanders:
Muhammad over Mesopotamia, Assyria, Armenia, and Azerbaijan;
and al-Hajjaj, his servant, over all of Persia and Arabia.
And while al-Hajjaj was ruthlessly plundering the leaders of the Arabs,
Muhammad sent and brought Mu'id (or: Mu'add?), the leader of the Christian Taghlibite Arabs,
and urged him to become a Muslim.
And when he was not willing,
he threw him into a pit of mire.
And again he brought him out and coaxed him.
And when he would not yield at all,
he killed him.
And he gathered again the leaders of the Armenians,
and shut them up in one of the churches of Armenia,
and set fire to it,
and burned them all.
And he killed Anastasius, son of Andrew, the governor of Edessa.
Nevertheless, Christian leaders were still directing the political affairs in the empire of the Arabs.
